title: Drama & Shakespeare
examples: What is the difference between an aside and a soliloquy?
How can Shakespeare build suspense on stage?
Can you give an example of dramatic irony in a play?

explain.say: Today we will look at three ways playwrights build drama. We will learn about stagecraft, soliloquy, and dramatic irony.
Stagecraft refers to the technical elements of a play. This includes the setting, costumes, and props used on stage.
A soliloquy is when a character speaks their thoughts aloud alone on stage. This lets the audience hear private feelings.
Dramatic irony happens when the audience knows something important the characters do not. This creates tension for us.
In a play, the playwright uses these techniques to build suspense. For example, the setting itself can create mood.
A common mistake is confusing an aside with a soliloquy. An aside is spoken to the audience, but a soliloquy is for the character's own thoughts.

items: Aside | To other characters or audience
Soliloquy | To oneself, unheard by others

faq.q: What is the main difference between an aside and a soliloquy?
faq.a: An aside is a brief remark meant for the audience or another character. A soliloquy is a long speech where a character reveals their deepest thoughts to the audience.
asks: Is an aside the same as a soliloquy?
How do I tell if it is an aside or a soliloquy?

faq.q: How does dramatic irony make the play more exciting?
faq.a: It builds suspense because the audience feels anxious knowing what the characters are about to face. This gap in knowledge keeps us watching.
asks: Why is it exciting when we know something they do not?
What is the effect of dramatic irony?

faq.a: No, stagecraft includes everything technical. This covers costumes, props, and the overall lighting and sound design too.
asks: Does stagecraft just mean the backdrop?
What elements are part of stagecraft?

faq.q: Does Shakespeare always use these techniques?
faq.a: While Shakespeare is famous for them, playwrights from all eras use these dramatic tools. They are fundamental parts of playwriting.
asks: Are these techniques only for Shakespeare?
Are these techniques old or new?

faq.q: If a character speaks to no one, is it a soliloquy?
faq.a: If the character is alone and speaking their thoughts, it is likely a soliloquy. If someone is present but they speak quietly, it might be an aside.
asks: What if the character is alone on stage?
When is it definitely a soliloquy?

facts: Stagecraft includes all technical aspects of a performance.
A soliloquy allows the audience direct access to a character's inner mind.
Dramatic irony occurs when the audience possesses superior knowledge to the characters.
Props are movable objects essential to the plot action.

quiz.say: A character speaks their deepest thoughts aloud while alone on stage. This technique is called:
quiz.show: A character speaks thoughts aloud alone.
quiz.why: A soliloquy is specifically designed for a character to reveal their private, deep thoughts to the audience.

wrong.1: An aside is a brief comment meant for others on stage, not a full outpouring of private thought.
wrong.2: Stagecraft refers to the physical elements like sets and costumes, not the speech act itself.
wrong.3: Dramatic irony is the situation where the audience knows more than the character.

quiz.say: The audience knows a secret that the main character does not know. This dramatic device is:
quiz.why: Dramatic irony is the specific literary term for the audience having superior knowledge to the characters.

wrong.0: An aside is a direct comment, usually brief, made to the audience or another character.
wrong.1: Stagecraft involves the physical elements like lighting or props, not the knowledge gap.
wrong.3: A soliloquy is a speech; it is the action of revealing thoughts, not the situation itself.

quiz.say: The use of a stormy setting and dark costumes helps build the mood. This element is part of:
quiz.why: Stagecraft covers all the technical elements, including setting and costumes, used to build atmosphere.

wrong.1: A soliloquy is a piece of dialogue, not a physical element like a stormy setting.
wrong.2: Dramatic irony is a knowledge gap, not a visual or physical element on stage.
wrong.3: An aside is a spoken line, which is different from the visual elements of the setting.
